seo_title: Charcuterie Boards for Dietary Needs & Kids: 3 Plans
h1: Charcuterie Board Ideas for Dietary Needs
link_text: boards for gluten-free, vegan and kids
description: Board plans built around a dietary need rather than adapted at the last minute: gluten-free, fully plant-based, and one built for children. What to buy, what to leave off, and how to serve a mixed table.
answer: Build the board around the restriction rather than removing things at the end. Most of a charcuterie board is already gluten-free and most of it is already safe for children; the problems sit in the crackers, a few processed meats, and anything with a choking risk.
intro: A board that was planned for the restriction looks like a board. A board that had things taken off it at the last minute looks like a board with gaps, and the person it was adapted for notices.

These three plans each start from the need. If you want the swap lists rather than a whole board, the dietary guides go through the ingredients one at a time and say what is safe, what is not and what to use instead.

ideas.heading: Gluten-free charcuterie board
ideas.intro: Aged cheese and prosciutto contain no gluten. The risk sits in the crackers, a few processed meats that use wheat as a binder, and crumbs falling from a shared cracker pile.

boards.name: Gluten-Free Charcuterie Board
boards.best_for: A coeliac guest at a mixed table
boards.blurb: Natural aged cheese and whole-muscle cured meat, with seed crackers and vegetables instead of wheat crackers. Serves 8 to 12 for $50 to $80.

ideas.heading: Vegan and plant-based board
ideas.intro: Cashew-based cheeses work for the same reason dairy does: cashews are rich and creamy, so a cashew brie spreads and coats the tongue the way the real thing does.

boards.name: Vegan Plant-Based Board
boards.blurb: Cashew brie and other plant cheeses, marinated vegetables, olives, nuts and fruit, with no dairy or meat anywhere on the board. $45 to $70.

ideas.heading: Kid-friendly board
ideas.intro: Children eat more of what they recognise. Leading with familiar shapes and mild flavours gets more eaten than a board of interesting cheeses does.

boards.name: Kid-Friendly Charcuterie Board
boards.blurb: Cheddar sticks, string cheese, pepperoni and rolled turkey, with fruit and simple crackers. Serves 8 to 10 for $35 to $55.

sections.heading: What is already gluten-free on a board

items.text: Natural aged cheese of any kind, prosciutto, jamon, bresaola and most whole-muscle cured meat, fresh and dried fruit, nuts, olives, honey and most jams.
Some salami and sausage use wheat as a binder or are dusted with flour, beer-washed cheeses, blue cheese made with bread-grown mould, and anything described as a spread or a dip.
Wheat crackers, baguette, crostini, pretzels and most biscuits for cheese.
If one guest is coeliac rather than avoiding gluten by choice, keep the wheat crackers on a separate plate with their own knife. Crumbs in a shared bowl of jam are enough to cause a reaction.

sections.heading: Serving a board to young children

items.lead: Choking risks to cut or leave off.
items.text: Whole grapes, whole cherry tomatoes, large olives with stones, round slices of hard sausage and whole nuts. Halve grapes and tomatoes lengthways for under-fives.
Mild cheddar, mozzarella, string cheese and turkey get eaten. Blue cheese, washed rind and strongly spiced salami usually do not.

items.lead: Give things a shape they know.
items.text: Sticks, cubes and rolled slices get picked up. A wedge broken off a wheel often does not.
Children tend to eat foods they can see individually. A board where everything touches gets eaten less than one with clear little groups.

sections.heading: Feeding a mixed table from one board

items.lead: Build the restricted board, then add.
items.text: Start with the version everyone can eat, then put the crackers, the dairy or the meat on a second plate beside it. Nobody is eating a lesser board that way.
A small card in front of the plant cheeses or the gluten-free crackers saves the guest having to ask, which is the part most people dislike.

items.lead: Give each one its own knife.
items.text: One knife moving between a dairy brie and a cashew brie undoes the point of having both.

faq.a: Most of it is. Natural aged cheese and whole-muscle cured meats like prosciutto contain no gluten. The gluten on a typical board comes from the crackers and bread, and occasionally from a salami that uses wheat as a binder.

faq.q: What crackers can I use for a gluten-free board?
faq.a: Seed and nut crackers, rice crackers, corn-based crisps, or no crackers at all: cucumber rounds, endive leaves and sliced apple all carry cheese perfectly well and add colour the crackers would not.

faq.q: How do I stop cross-contamination on a shared board?
faq.a: Keep wheat crackers on their own plate rather than on the board, give every soft cheese and jam its own knife or spoon, and serve the gluten-free crackers first before crumbs are in the air.

faq.q: What should I leave off a board for toddlers?
faq.a: Whole grapes, whole cherry tomatoes, whole nuts, olives with stones and coin-shaped slices of hard sausage are the common choking risks. Halve round fruit lengthways and cut meat into strips rather than circles.

faq.q: Can one board work for vegans and meat eaters?
faq.a: Yes, if you build the plant-based board first and put the cheese and meat on a separate plate beside it. Doing it the other way round leaves the vegan guest eating the gaps.

faq.q: Do plant-based cheeses actually work on a board?
faq.a: Cashew-based ones do. Cashews are rich and creamy in the way dairy is, so a cashew brie spreads and coats the tongue similarly. Coconut-oil-based slices behave less like cheese and are better melted than served cold.
